name: Question 5
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14061629/assets/9684a8beb9981ac024d56d7467672b66c73eeb90c8dcaae11e61c0686dc1fcde.png)

Which of the following gives the line integral ${\int }_{C}(4x-2y)\,\text{d}s,$ where the curve $C$ is three-quarters of the ellipse $16{x}^{2}+4{y}^{2}=64,$ shown above?
worked_solution:
We will use the formula

$$
{\int }_{C}f(x,y)\,\text{d}s={\int }_{a}^{b}f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t.
$$

 

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form

$$
\frac{{x}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}+\frac{{y}^{2}}{{4}^{2}}=1.
$$

So, the curve $C$ is an ellipse centered at $O$ with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of $2$ and $4,$ respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as 

$$
r(t)=⟨2\operatorname{cos}⁡t,\,4\operatorname{sin}⁡t⟩,\,-\frac{\pi }{2}\le t\le \pi .
$$

Computing ${r}^{′}(t)$ and $‖{r}^{′}(t)‖,$ we get following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{r}^{′}(t) & =\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}\,i+\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}\,j \\  & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)i+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t)j \\  & =-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t\,i+4\operatorname{cos}⁡t\,j \\ ‖{r}^{′}(t)‖ & =\sqrt{{(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})}^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{(-2\operatorname{sin}⁡t)^{2}+(4\operatorname{cos}⁡t)^{2}} \\  & =\sqrt{4{sin}^{2}⁡t+16{cos}^{2}⁡t} \\  & =\sqrt{12{cos}^{2}⁡t+4({sin}^{2}⁡t+{cos}^{2}⁡t)} \\  & =\sqrt{12{cos}^{2}⁡t+4} \\  & =2\sqrt{3{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\end{aligned}
$$

Now, since $f(x,y)=4x-2y,$ we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}f(r(t)) & =4(2\operatorname{cos}⁡t)-2(4\operatorname{sin}⁡t) \\  & =8\operatorname{cos}⁡t-8\operatorname{sin}⁡t \\  & =8(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can write the integral as

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}(4x-2y)\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }f(r(t))\,‖{r}^{′}(t)‖\,\text{d}t \\  & ={\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }8(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\cdot 2\sqrt{3{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t \\  & =16{\int }_{-\pi /2}^{\pi }(\operatorname{cos}⁡t-\operatorname{sin}⁡t)\sqrt{3{cos}^{2}⁡t+1}\,\text{d}t.\end{aligned}
$$

Question 5
?

Which of the following gives the line integral ∫C(4x−2y)ds, where the curve C is three-quarters of the ellipse 16x2+4y2=64, shown above?

a
4∫−π/2π(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)3cos2⁡t+1dt
b
8∫03π/2(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)cos2⁡t+3dt
c
16∫03π/2(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)3cos2⁡t+1dt
d
16∫−π/2π(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)3cos2⁡t+1dt
e
8∫−π/2π(cos⁡t+sin⁡t)cos2⁡t+3dt
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We will use the formula ∫Cf(x,y)ds=∫abf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt.

Note that we can write the equation of our ellipse in the form x222+y242=1.

So, the curve C is an ellipse centered at O with horizontal and vertical semiaxes of 2 and 4, respectively. Therefore, it can be parametrized as r(t)=⟨2cos⁡t,4sin⁡t⟩,−π2≤t≤π.

Computing r′(t) and ‖r′(t)‖, we get following: r′(t)=dxdti+dydtj=ddt(2cos⁡t)i+ddt(4sin⁡t)j=−2sin⁡ti+4cos⁡tj‖r′(t)‖=(dxdt)2+(dydt)2=(−2sin⁡t)2+(4cos⁡t)2=4sin2⁡t+16cos2⁡t=12cos2⁡t+4(sin2⁡t+cos2⁡t)=12cos2⁡t+4=23cos2⁡t+1

Now, since f(x,y)=4x−2y, we obtain f(r(t))=4(2cos⁡t)−2(4sin⁡t)=8cos⁡t−8sin⁡t=8(cos⁡t−sin⁡t).

Therefore, we can write the integral as ∫C(4x−2y)ds=∫−π/2πf(r(t))‖r′(t)‖dt=∫−π/2π8(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)⋅23cos2⁡t+1dt=16∫−π/2π(cos⁡t−sin⁡t)3cos2⁡t+1dt.
